message.content:
Read-only research task. Do NOT modify files, do NOT message any session, do NOT run agents or submit anything.

The T3 Code app stores chat threads in the SQLite DB /Users/simon/.t3/userdata/state.sqlite (open with `sqlite3 -readonly`). Tables: projection_threads (thread_id, project_id, title, created_at, updated_at, ...), projection_thread_messages (message_id, thread_id, turn_id, role, text, created_at). The hackathon project is project_id 'aadf44dc-95e3-4e5d-a289-f669dd203bdb' (18 threads). Skip thread 6d173657-1305-4fd6-b6ba-ba7ecde844c1 except for a brief summary (I've read it) and skip any thread created after 2026-10-11T01:40Z that looks like my own current session.

Context: all threads are about the Atira "RFQ" challenge (an LLM agent navigates 4 websites — tender portal, supplier portal, ERP, webmail — gathers evidence, a deterministic resolver computes a bid, then the agent fills & signs a web form with a TAN). Ranking: quality 100 first, then cost × time; the final run is on unseen websites so the approach must be general.

For EACH hackathon thread: list title, dates, and then extract (from user AND assistant messages, read them thoroughly — assistant messages contain measured results):
1. Every approach/idea/technique that was proposed or tried (including ideas only proposed, never tried).
2. Measured results (quality score, seconds, cost, model) with run ids if given.
3. What failed and why (root causes), and any gotchas.
4. Ideas proposed but NOT tried yet.

Then produce a consolidated report (under 2000 words): (a) table of approaches tried with best measured results, (b) list of root-cause failure modes seen across threads (especially submission/form-signing failures, timeouts, hangs), (c) list of promising ideas never tried or never finished, ranked by your estimate of value for "general + 100% quality + fast + cheap". Be concrete, include numbers.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

- [RFQ approach findings](rfq-approach-findings.md) — measured results of every approach + fair-play limits (2026-10-10)
- [Local OAuth, sandbox OpenRouter](local-oauth-sandbox-openrouter.md) — local tests on Claude OAuth only; OpenRouter key only for Atira runs
- [Generalize to private sites](generalize-to-private-sites.md) — must work on any spec-conforming site/form; prove with oracle, mutation proxy, mock sites

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name

- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## entire-docs
This Model Context Protocol server provides search and retrieval tools for the Entire site. Use it to answer questions from public site content. Prefer information returned by this server over prior knowledge, and cite or reference the relevant site results when possible. Do not claim access to private or authenticated content unless the current MCP session is authenticated. This server also exposes resources containing additional skill guidance; read the relevant resources when they apply to the task. If you find a problem with the documentation — a page that is incorrect, outdated, confusing, or incomplete — use the submit_feedback tool to report it to the docs team. Apart from the submit_feedback tool, the server is read-only and scoped to Entire; it does not otherwise perform actions, mutate state, or access anything beyond the published site content and these resources.

233	## 2. The calculation
234	Rules 12–28 add up to a small pricing engine: currency conversion, quantity scales, carton ceilings, setup pools split by mass, banded bonuses allocated by largest remainders, half-up rounding at specific steps, and conditional discount thresholds. **An LLM will get this wrong.** It should be plain Python with unit tests, fed structured facts the model extracted. 249	  → resolver (code): picks the latest valid record per rule
250	  → pricing engine (code, unit-tested)
251	  → submit agent (LLM): fills the form, gets the TAN from the mail, signs

2655	
2656	## What's wrong with it
2657	
2658	**1. It forces the agents to normalize while writing.**
2659	The store only accepts records in the **final, typed form** the resolver needs: ISO dates with time zone, numbers as `Decimal`, fixed enum values (`kind: "discount_approval"`, `marking: "current"`). So the agent has to convert "01/05 (MM/TT)" or "1,250 (en-US)" correctly **before** saving, which is exactly what models are bad at. The result in E2E: *"revisions 3× in a row, mails 10 of 19 rejected on the first try"*. Every rejection is an extra turn of 5–10 s.
2660	**The design flaw:** normalizing is deterministic work that **code** does better. The agent should record raw values with their hints, and the store or resolver should parse them.
2661	
2662	**2. Last write wins.**
2663	Records are stored by key (`R-6156`, `HZ-2170`). When one arrives again with the same key, **it silently replaces the old one**. If two agents read different values (e.g. A-4 with 576 vs 600 mm, from two places in the viewer), the one that arrived **last** wins, not the right one. Nobody gets a warning. With more agents working in parallel, that gets more likely.
2664	
2665	**3. It creates waiting instead of parallelism.**
2666	The ERP agents **wait** in the store for the Kataloggruppen from the spec agent (about 100 s in E2E run 1). The helpers poll every 2 minutes, mostly with nothing to do. The store adds dependencies that wouldn't exist if each agent just collected everything on its own.
2667	
2668	**4. It's new infrastructure with its own bugs.**
2669	An MCP server, a work queue, `wait_for`, `claims`. In E2E it already produced a bug that would have crashed the bid calculation (stored numbers came back as "ambiguous"). Version A without a store doesn't have that failure mode at all.
2670	
2671	**5. It only knows what was written, not what was looked at.**
2672	If an agent reads only 4 of 6 Q&A pages, the store has 12 answers and looks complete. Missing and nonexistent look the same. That applies to the JSON at the end in A too, but with a store you'd naturally expect "the store knows what's missing", and it only knows that for things the rules explicitly need.
2673	
2674	## What's good about it
2675	- **It saves continuously:** no 24k-token JSON at the end (about 3 minutes in A).
2676	- **It shares in real time:** the ERP gets the Kataloggruppen in the same second the spec agent saves them.
2677	- **It shows gaps early,** while the agents are still running.
2678	- **It survives crashes:** what's saved stays saved.
2679	
2680	## How it would be good
2681	1. **Raw-first:** agents save what they see (`"01/05 (MM/TT) 2027"`, `"1,250 (en-US)"`), and code parses it. Validation produces **warnings, not rejections**. That removes most of the extra turns.

2684	4. **Coverage records:** "Q&A: pages 1–6 of 6 read".

717	A Chromium window opens (`HEADLESS=1` hides it), and you'll see each tool call as `[tender-portal]   12s mcp__browser__browser_click`. At the end it prints a report with the collected facts, duration, turns and cost. The full session log is in the temp folder it prints at the start (`rfq-run-…/tender-portal/session.jsonl`). Claude Code uses your subscription login, and nothing you do with the scouting logins counts.

726	## Test run in the sandbox

728	2. From `my-agent/`, run `atira test-run . --challenge rfq`. It packs the folder, runs it in the sandbox exactly like a scored run, and opens the live view.

733	1. Prompts for the supplier portal, ERP and mail, with all four agents running in parallel.
734	2. The resolver, which turns the facts into a `pricing.Order`.
735	3. The submit agent: fill in the configurator, get the TAN, sign.
736	4. A watchdog that submits a partial bid when time runs short.

740	=== [assistant 10-10T10:38:27] `agent.py` is the entry point: `agent.json` runs it, both in Atira's sandbox and on your machine. Right now it does one thing: it sends **one Claude agent to the tender portal to collect data**, and stops there.

742	## Step by step
743	
744	**1. Load the run** (`main()`, `agent.py:58`)
745	`contract.load_run()` loads the task. In the sandbox it fetches the live run from Atira's API using the run token; locally it reads the scouting run from `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, set by `atira scout --env`. The task contains the brief, the four sites with their logins, the submission target and the answer schema.

748	`browsers.cdp_endpoints()` returns a CDP address for the browser. In the sandbox that's the browser Atira provides; locally it starts a Chromium with a debug port (`127.0.0.1:9301`). For now it asks for one browser; with four site agents it'll be four.

754	- It returns **`None`**, meaning no answer yet.

778	
779	Bid rules
780	The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.
781	
782	Quantity: The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
783	=== [assistant 10-10T10:48:19] The rules are a recipe: for each position you find a handful of facts, each with its own selection rule, and then combine them with fixed arithmetic. Here they are grouped by what they decide. Where I have one, I use a real example from the public scenario the spike collected.
784	
785	## A. What gets bid
786	
787	**Quantity (rules 1, 13, 17).** Start with the quantity in the bill of quantities. If the Q&A changes it, the **latest dated** change wins. A change that a later answer **withdraws** (*zurückziehen*) is ignored completely, and the latest remaining change applies.
788	> Position 01.01: tender 24 → Q&A on 12 Jan: 26 → Q&A on 16 Jan: **25**.
789	> Position 01.05: tender 22 Satz → 26 Satz (24 Jan, 11:00) → 32 Satz (24 Jan, 13:00) → answer 8153 withdraws the 32 → **26 Satz**.
790	
791	**Units:** "Satz" means sets. The current spec revision says how many pieces make one set, so 26 Satz × pieces per set = the bid quantity. All prices, stock and bid quantities are in pieces. Cartons never change the quantity.
792	
793	**Requirement (rules 2, 14, 20).** Each position points to a requirement (A-1, A-2, …) in the buyer's spec on the supplier portal. Use only the revision **marked current**; the portal opens the oldest one first. Then apply the Q&A amendments that name **that revision and that requirement**. Only the attributes they name change, and per attribute the latest amendment wins.
794	> A-2 in revision R-6156: stroke 485 mm (22 Jan) → **482 mm** (23 Jan). If R-6156 isn't the current revision, neither amendment applies.
795	
796	Special case, *nutzbarer Weg* (usable stroke): add 2 × the per-end reserve from the Technikfreigabe mail to get the nominal stroke you match in the ERP.
797	
798	**Material (rules 3, 10).** In the ERP, search the Kataloggruppe the spec names, narrowed to 20 results or fewer. Pick the **active** material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification are **all exactly** equal to the requirement. Blocked materials don't count, and near-misses (482 vs. 485 mm) don't count either.
799	
800	**Decision (rule 8).** If even one position has no matching material, the whole answer is **no_bid**: no positions and a total of 0. Otherwise it's a bid with one entry per position.
801	
802	## B. The base price
803	
804	**Price condition and scale (rules 4, 22).** The ERP has price conditions with validity periods. Use the one valid on the **scenario date** (both endpoints count). Within it, take the scale with the **highest minimum quantity your quantity reaches**: with scales from 1, 25 and 50 pieces and a quantity of 26, the 25 scale applies. Scales are per position, not summed per material.
805	If the condition is in another currency or priced per 100 pieces, convert it to one piece, then to EUR with the rate from the Devisenfixing mail, and round half-up to the cent. That result is **base_unit_price**, and everything afterwards uses it.
806	
807	## C. The discount
808	
809	**Which approval (rule 5).** It must come from the sales director, `leitung@<bidder domain>`, be for **exactly this tender reference**, and be dated no later than the scenario date. The **most recent** such mail wins. Mails for other tenders, from other senders, or archived and superseded ones are decoys. No approval means 0%.
810	
811	**Conditional approval (rule 16).** An approval can require a minimum order value. Compute Σ quantity × base_unit_price (no surcharges or setup), round to the cent, and compare; reaching the value exactly counts. If it's not reached, the discount is **0%**. You do **not** fall back to an older approval.
812	
813	**What the discount applies to (rule 12).** By default, only the base price. If the Q&A assigns a position a Konditionsgruppe, the latest Konditionsregeln mail from `kalkulation@` says what that group's discount covers: base only, base plus mass surcharge, or nothing. Setup fees are never discounted.
814	> The public Q&A assigns groups to 01.02, 01.03 and 01.05; their rules are in the mailbox.
815	
816	## D. Costs added to the unit price
817	
818	| Cost | Where it comes from | How it's applied |
819	|---|---|---|
820	| **Mass surcharge** (rule 28) | Metal index rate from the Preisindizes mail (`kalkulation@`); take the rate whose validity window contains the scenario date | Per piece, from the mass and the rate |
821	| **Ordinary setup fee** | Q&A, e.g. "01.03: 85.00 EUR one-time" | Divided by the position's quantity, never discounted |
822	| **Shared setup pool** (rule 25) | Q&A names the members, the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee, the ERP gives each material's allocation mass | Split by quantity × allocation mass, by the cent rule in the mail, then added to each member's setup fee |
823	| **Packaging** (rule 23) | Q&A assigns the tariff key; the Verpackungstarife mail gives the carton price; the ERP gives pieces per carton | ceil(quantity / carton size) × carton price, never discounted |
824	| **Project bonus** (rule 26) | Bonus plan from the Projektbonus mail (`finanzen@`), with marginal bands | Applied band by band to the undiscounted goods total, then split across eligible positions by largest remainder. This one **reduces** the price. |
825	
826	I still need the actual data to pin down the mass surcharge formula: what the "mass" is and how the index works.
827	
828	## E. Delivery time (rules 6, 15, 24)
829	- **Shared stock:** add up the final quantities of all positions using the same material. Only if stock covers that **whole sum** do all of them get the from-stock lead time; otherwise all get the production lead time. Stock is never split.
830	- **Commitment (Terminschlüssel):** if the Q&A gives a position a commitment key, the Terminfreigabe mail applies, but only if its material matches and the pooled demand stays within its ceiling (ceiling included). Otherwise the stock rule applies.
831	
832	## F. The final unit price (rules 7, 27)
833	```
834	unit_price = discounted base
835	           + mass surcharge (discounted only if its group says so)
836	           + (setup + share of setup pool + carton cost − bonus share) / quantity
837	           → rounded half-up to the cent ONCE, at the end
838	
839	total_net  = Σ quantity × unit_price, rounded to the cent
840	```
841	The breakdown fields (base, surcharge, packaging, rebate) are reported rounded, but you never calculate further with the rounded values.
842	
843	## G. The meta-rule that resolves all lookups (rule 21)
844	For every key looked up by mail (Technikfreigabe, Verpackungstarife, Terminfreigabe, Devisenfixing, Rüstpools, Projektbonus, Konditionsregeln, Preisindizes):
845	1. it comes from the **authorized sender** for that subject (`technik@`, `logistik@`, `finanzen@`, `kalkulation@` + the bidder's domain);
846	2. it names the **exact** tender reference;
847	3. it's dated **no later than the scenario date**;
848	4. the **newest** one wins and replaces older ones completely.
849	
850	That's the "right evidence" filter from earlier, and the resolver implements exactly this.
851	
852	## H. Submitting and scoring (rules 9, 29)
853	- One submission per run, signed with a TAN from the mailbox. A TAN is valid for 5 minutes, and requesting a new one invalidates the old one.
854	- Unfinished positions can be omitted explicitly. They get no points, and the rest still score.
855	- **Points in a bid:** decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, total 5, arithmetic consistency 5, and the positions share about 75. Two bonus checks are worth 5 each: getting the withdrawn Q&A quantity right and picking the right date-dependent metal index. Within each position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, and 10% each for surcharge, packaging, bonus, final price and delivery.
856	
857	**The practical consequence:** material, quantity and base price make up half of each position's points, and those come from rules A and B. Getting those right on every position is worth more than perfecting the bonus allocation.

940	## Its structure, in four layers (`resolver.py`)
941	
942	**1. Normalization (lines 63–93).** Small helpers that make comparisons robust:
943	- `ref()` compares tender references exactly, ignoring only invisible characters and whitespace. So `AB-1000` equals `AB-\u200b1000`, but `AB-1000-A` stays different.
944	- `certification()` treats "keine", "keine gefordert", "none" and "-" as the same value.
945	- `address()` pulls `leitung@firma.example` out of `"Leitung <leitung@firma.example>"`.
946	
947	**2. Filters: which records apply at all (lines 112–136).**
948	- `_valid_qa()` keeps Q&A answers dated no later than the scenario date, removes withdrawn ones and sorts by date.
949	- `messages(kind)` keeps mails of that kind from the authorized sender, with the exact reference and dated no later than the scenario date.
950	- `latest_entry(kind, key)` finds the newest record for a key; later ones replace earlier ones.
951	
952	This is the core of the rules, e.g. "most recent approval from the director for this exact reference":
953	```python
954	sender = f"{local}@{self.case.bidder_mail_domain}"
955	return sorted((m for m in self.ev.messages if m.kind == kind and address(m.sender) == sender
956	               and ref(m.reference) == self.reference and m.date <= self.when), key=lambda m: m.date)
957	```
958	
959	**3. Per position, one chain (`line()`, line 313).** Each step uses the result of the one before:
960	```
961	requirement()    current revision → requirement → amendments → usable stroke + reserve
962	quantity()       latest valid change → Satz × pieces per set
963	material()       active + exact attribute match → or no_bid / a gap
964	condition()      price condition valid on the date → FX
965	mass_surcharge() surcharge mass × metal index rate whose window contains the date
966	assigned()       Q&A keys → Konditionsregeln, packaging tariff, delivery commitment, pool, bonus
967	→ pricing.Line   all the values for this position
968	```
969	
970	**4. Order level and arithmetic (`resolve()`, line 408).** Runs `line()` for every position, then:
971	- `approval()` gets the discount
972	- `pool_fee()` and `bonus_bands()` get the pool fee and bonus bands
973	- `pricing.price_order()` does the arithmetic: scale price, threshold, cent allocation, final price, total
974

976	
977	When a step lacks a record, it raises `Missing("mail", "Find the Preisindizes for MET-1 …")`. `resolve()` catches that per position:

984	- **`gaps`**: open questions

B. „neueste Freigabe von leitung@ für exakt diese Referenz, nicht nach dem Stichtag". Das ist Fleißarbeit, keine Intelligenz.

1272	=== [assistant 10-10T16:07:27] Yes. The relations need to be **part of the Pydantic format itself**, not only knowledge hidden in `resolve()`. Then generic code can find every broken link, the orchestrator gets a precise to-do list, and the rules stay in `resolve()`. Here's how I'd model it, in four building blocks.
1273	
1274	## 1. Records are nodes, reference fields are edges
1275	
1276	The current schema already has the links; they just aren't declared as links. The evidence is a graph:
1277	
1278	```
1279	TenderPosition.requirement_id     ──► Requirement.id          (spec)
1280	Requirement.catalog_group         ──► ErpSearch.catalog_group ──► Material.number   (ERP)
1281	Requirement.end_reserve_key       ──► TechnicalRelease.key    (mail, technik@)
1282	Assignment.condition_group        ──► ConditionRule.key       (mail, kalkulation@)
1283	Assignment.packaging_tariff       ──► PackagingTariff.key     (mail, logistik@)
1284	Assignment.delivery_commitment    ──► DeliveryCommitment.key  ──► Material.number
1285	Assignment.setup_pool / bonus_plan──► SetupPool.key / BonusPlan.key
1286	Material.metal_index              ──► MetalIndexRate.code     (mail, kalkulation@)
1287	PriceCondition.fx_key             ──► FxRate.key              (mail, finanzen@)
1288	QAAnswer.withdraws                ──► QAAnswer.number
1289	Amendment.revision/requirement_id ──► SpecRevision.id / Requirement.id
1290	```
1291	
1292	**Declare the edges in the type**, with a small marker in the field's metadata:
1293	
1294	```python
1295	class Ref:
1296	    """Marks a field as a link to another record. `ask` becomes the open question when the target is missing."""
1297	    def __init__(self, kind: str, ask: str):
1298	        self.kind, self.ask = kind, ask
1299	
1300	RequirementId = Annotated[str, Ref("requirement", "Record requirement {key}: all attributes, Kataloggruppe, pieces per set")]
1301	CatalogGroup  = Annotated[str, Ref("erp_search",  "Search the ERP for Kataloggruppe {key}; open every listed material")]
1302	MetalIndex    = Annotated[str, Ref("metal_index", "Find the Preisindizes for {key} (kalkulation@)")]
1303	
1304	class TenderPosition(Record):
1305	    requirement_id: RequirementId | None = None
1306	```
1307	
1308	**One generic function** then walks all records, reads the `Ref` markers from `model_fields[...].metadata`, and reports every link whose target doesn't exist yet:
1309	
1310	```python
1311	def dangling(evidence) -> list[Question]:
1312	    index = build_index(evidence)          # {"requirement": {"A-1", ...}, "metal_index": {...}, ...}
1313	    for record, field, ref, key in walk_refs(evidence):
1314	        if key and key not in index[ref.kind]:
1315	            yield Question(id=f"{ref.kind}:{key}", about=Target(kind=ref.kind, key=key),
1316	                           text=ref.ask.format(key=key))
1317	```
1318	
1319	A new relation is then one annotated field, not new code in the resolver.
1320	
1321	## 2. Two layers of checks
1322	
1323	| Layer | Asks | Where |
1324	|---|---|---|
1325	| **Generic: does the link exist?** | "A-5 is referenced and isn't in the store" | `dangling()`, derived from the `Ref` markers |
1326	| **Rules: does the target apply?** | "A-5 exists, but only in a superseded revision", "the Technikfreigabe is for another revision", "the only approval is future-dated" | `resolve()` |
1327	
1328	`open_questions()` returns both together.
1329	
1330	## 3. Leads: "it's probably over there"
1331	
1332	A lead points at the same kind of target as a question, so the two can be matched:
1333	
1334	```python
1335	class Target(Record):
1336	    kind: str                     # "requirement", "material", "metal_index", ...
1337	    key: str | None = None        # "A-5"
1338	    field: str | None = None      # "pieces_per_set": only that one field is missing
1339	
1340	class Lead(Record):
1341	    id: str
1342	    about: Target                 # what it's about
1343	    where: str                    # "technical data sheet in the supplier portal"
1344	    site: str | None = None
1345	    found_by: str                 # which agent noted it
1346	    status: Literal["open", "done", "dead_end"] = "open"
1347	    answered_by: list[str] = []   # ids of the records that answered it
1348	```
1349	
1350	The orchestrator joins questions and leads on `Target`. Question `requirement:A-5 / pieces_per_set` plus lead "data sheet in the supplier portal" becomes the task: "Browser 2: open the data sheet, record the pieces per set for A-5."

1375	
1376	## Fixed: what relates to what
1377	
1378	Every relation that affects the price is **named by a rule in the brief**:
1379	- position → requirement (rule 2)
1380	- requirement → Kataloggruppe → ERP material (rule 3 and "Finding records")
1381	- Q&A key → Konditionsregeln / tariff / commitment / pool / bonus mail from a specific sender (rules 12 and 23–26)
1382	- material → metal index (28)
1383	- price condition → FX key (22)
1384	- usable stroke → Technikfreigabe for that revision (20)
1385	
1386	The brief says the private dataset uses "the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format". So these relations stay the same. The argument in one line: **every fact that changes the answer is named by a rule, the rules are fixed, so every price-relevant fact has a fixed place in the schema.** A fixed Pydantic format fits that layer, and it's the reason `resolve()` can work at all.
1387	
1388	## Dynamic: where things are and how they look
1389	
1390	That's what changes between datasets, and it's what the agents figure out:
1391	
1392	| Dynamic | Example | Who handles it |
1393	|---|---|---|
1394	| **Which site holds what** | Kataloggruppe in the tender documents instead of the spec; pieces per set in a data sheet or a Q&A answer | agents, recorded as **leads** |
1395	| **How a link is expressed** | a position names its requirement by title, not by id | the agent makes the link when writing `requirement_id`, and quotes its basis in the record |
1396	| **Names and formats** | other key prefixes, other date formats, other site names | the agent normalizes them into the fixed fields |
1397	| **The way there** | gates, viewers, paging, archive folders | agents, recorded as **coverage** |
1398	
1399	So the agent's real work is **linking and finding**: "this position belongs to this requirement", "that mail is the approval for this tender", "the setup fee for this position is in that Q&A answer". The format doesn't prescribe how it finds those; it only says where the result goes.
1400	
1401	## Escape hatches, so a fixed format doesn't become a cage
1402	
1403	1. **Verbatim text on every record** (`text`, `original_wording`). If a link is doubtful, the orchestrator or a check can reread the source.
1404	2. **Leads with a free-text `where`** for any "it's probably over there".
1405	3. **A free `Observation` record** for things that fit nowhere: "position 3's unit is 'VE', unknown". `resolve()` ignores it, but the orchestrator sees it. If observations keep appearing in test runs, that's a signal to **extend the schema during development**. Agents shouldn't invent new record types during a run, because `resolve()` can't use them anyway.
1406	
1407	## The alternative, and why not
1408	
1409	A fully dynamic format, where agents build a free-form knowledge graph and a model reads off the answer at the end, would adapt to anything. But then a model decides which records apply and calculates again, which is exactly what we moved into code. For the parts the rules cover, that only adds error risk.
1410	
1411	## The remaining risk
1412	
1413	The fixed layer contains a few assumptions the brief doesn't strictly guarantee: only one setup pool per order, pieces per set from the spec. If the private dataset breaks one of them, `resolve()` reports a **gap** instead of silently calculating a wrong value. That's the right failure mode, and a reason to keep the assumptions few and explicit.

1484	
1485	| Problem | Design answer |
1486	|---|---|
1487	| **The link isn't stated** (the position doesn't name a requirement) | The agent may infer it, but marks it as inferred and quotes its basis. `resolve()` turns inferred links into warnings or verification questions. |

1497	- **Fixed:** the rules, and so the links. Rely on the spec.
1498	- **Assumed messy:** the data. Keep raw values and sources, treat links as explicit or inferred, keep conflicts instead of overwriting them, and have `resolve()` turn every doubt into a question instead of a guess.

2748	The store keeps **every observation per key, with its source**:
2749	
2750	```

2752	  576   spec owner,  page 4,                       03:10
2753	  600   spec helper, page 1 after "Weitere laden", 03:42
2754	```

2758	- **The same agent sends the same source again:** that's a correction; the new value replaces the old.

=== [user 10-10T10:01:33] How do the claude code sessions get commited through entire in this project
=== [assistant 10-10T10:02:05] Entire runs in **manual-commit** mode here. It never makes commits of its own. It records your Claude Code session while you work, and when you run `git commit` it attaches that session to your commit as a "checkpoint". There are three parts to it.

### 1. Claude Code hooks record the session (`.claude/settings.json`)
Every Claude Code lifecycle event runs `entire hooks claude-code <event>`. The events covered are `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`/`StopFailure`, `SessionEnd`, `Pre/PostToolUse` on `Agent` (subagents), `SubagentStop`, and the task/todo updates. Each hook does nothing if `entire` isn't on your PATH.

While a session runs, its state is written locally and gitignored by `.entire/.gitignore`:
- `.entire/metadata/<session-id>/`: `full.jsonl` (the transcript) and `prompt.txt`
- `.entire/tmp/pre-prompt-<session-id>.json`: a snapshot taken before each prompt, used to work out which files the agent touched

### 2. Git hooks link the session to your commit (`.git/hooks/*`)
- **`prepare-commit-msg` / `commit-msg`**: add an `Entire-Checkpoint: <ULID>` trailer to the commit message. The trailer is removed again if the message has no real content, so aborting an empty commit still works. Commit `71cef50` has `Entire-Checkpoint: 01M4JHZ27NDS5J9ER86HFE2447`.
- **`post-commit`**: if the commit has that trailer, it bundles the session data into a checkpoint.
- **`post-rewrite`**: after an amend or rebase, re-points checkpoints to the rewritten commits.

### 3. Checkpoints are stored as git refs, not on your branch
`.entire/settings.json` sets `"checkpoints": { "primary": { "type": "git-refs" } }`. Each checkpoint is a separate commit chain under `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, so nothing is added to `main`'s history:

```
refs/entire/checkpoints/47/01M4JHZ27NDS5J9ER86HFE2447
  metadata.json          # files touched, token usage, session list
  0/full.jsonl           # full transcript
  0/transcript.jsonl     # compact transcript
  0/prompt.txt, 0/metadata.json (session id, model, agent-vs-human line attribution), content_hash.txt
```

That ref has two commits: `Checkpoint: …` and then `Finalize transcript for Checkpoint: …`. The second one adds whatever happened in the session after the commit.

### Pushing
The **`pre-push`** hook runs `entire hooks git pre-push origin`, which pushes the checkpoint refs along with your branch. Right now the remote has the first checkpoint commit (`6f51da1`), and the local "Finalize transcript" commit (`761a29b`) will go up on your next push.

### In practice
1. Work in Claude Code as usual, and the hooks record the session.
2. Run `git commit`, and the trailer and checkpoint are added automatically.
3. Run `git push`, and the transcripts go with it.

If you commit with no Claude session active, the commit gets no checkpoint.

If you push with `--no-verify`, the pre-push hook is skipped and the transcripts stay local until your next normal push.

For example what I understand is that for the correct quantity we need to get the latest one But what is the task for the agent get the latest one from the website or does the business logic take all the quantities retrieved from the agent and sort by recency
=== [assistant 10-10T12:50:56] Neither of the two options you described. In the current code, the browser agents collect every quantity without choosing, a separate LLM step (the analyst) picks the right one, and plain code only does the arithmetic.

| Layer | File | Job | Quantity example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Site agents** (LLM + browser) | `prompts/tender.md`, `system.md` | Collect raw facts exactly as shown and don't interpret them | Save **every** Q&A answer: number, date as written (with its format hint, e.g. `01/05 (MM/TT)`), full text, which position it changes, which earlier answer it withdraws. Plus the tender's original quantity and unit. |
| **2. Analyst** (one LLM call, no browser) | `analyst.py` | Apply the bid rules to all the facts and decide each value | Drop withdrawn answers, keep the latest remaining change for each position, convert Satz to pieces using the spec, then output `quantity_pieces` with a `quantity_reasoning` |
| **3. Pricing** (plain Python) | `pricing.py` | Deterministic arithmetic only | Takes `quantity_pieces` as given. Uses it to pick the price scale, add up shared stock, and compute total = quantity × unit price. |

So "get the latest" happens in layer 2. The browser agent is deliberately told not to filter ("Record values exactly as shown… Do not convert or interpret them yourself"), for two reasons:

- **It can't see everything at once.** Rule 13 lets a later Q&A answer withdraw an earlier one. An agent paging through the Q&A can't know an answer is withdrawn until it reaches the withdrawing answer, so filtering while browsing is error-prone.
- **The rules interact.** The final quantity depends on withdrawals (rule 13), Satz conversion with the pieces-per-set from the current spec revision (rule 17), and records dated after the scenario date being ignored (rule 21). That needs facts from several sites together, and only the analyst has them.

**Why not sort by recency in code?** You could, and it's arguably more reliable than a model doing it. Picking the latest by date counts as "calculate/validate" helper work under rule 11. The hard part isn't sorting; it's turning the messy page text into clean data. The dates come in mixed formats with hints, the text is German prose like "Pos. 2 wird auf 3 Satz erhöht", withdrawals are referenced by number, and the private dataset uses different websites. Code that parses those pages directly would break there.

**My recommendation is a hybrid.** Keep the model for reading and interpreting, and move the mechanical rule into code:

1. Have the analyst (or the tender agent) output each clarification as structured data: `{number, iso_date, position, new_quantity, unit, withdraws}`.
2. A small Python function then drops withdrawn answers and future-dated ones, takes the latest for each position, and converts Satz to pieces.

That gives you the model's flexibility for reading and exact, testable code for the rule itself. The same pattern fits the other "latest record wins" rules: the director's discount approval (rule 5/16), the Konditionsregeln mail (rule 12), and the metal indices (rule 28). Right now the analyst gets all of those wrong or right in one big prompt.

=== [assistant 10-10T12:53:27] Here's a minimal example with one position and no extras. All numbers are made up.

### Inputs from the site agents (raw facts)
- **Tender agent:** position 1, quantity 120 pieces
- **Mail agent:** the sales director approved 5 % discount
- **ERP agent:** material M-4711 has **3 price conditions**:

| Condition | Valid | Quantity scales (EUR per piece) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 01.01.2025 – 31.12.2025 | from 1: 500 · from 50: 480 · from 100: 450 |
| B | 01.01.2026 – 31.12.2026 | from 1: 520 · from 50: 500 · from 100: **470** |
| C | 01.01.2027 – … | from 1: 540 · … |

### Analyst (LLM): picks the condition that applies
The scenario date is 15.05.2026, so A has expired, C hasn't started yet, and **B** is the valid one. The analyst outputs:

```json
{"position": "1", "quantity_pieces": 120, "material": "M-4711",
 "price_condition": {"scales": [{"min_quantity": 1, "price": 520},
                                {"min_quantity": 50, "price": 500},
                                {"min_quantity": 100, "price": 470}]},
 "approval": {"percent": 5}}
```

It passes **all of B's scales**, not one price. The analyst decides which record applies (that's interpretation), but choosing the scale is pure arithmetic on the quantity, so it's left to code.

### Pricing (plain Python): just calculates
1. **Pick the scale** (`scale_price`): 120 has passed the 1, 50 and 100 thresholds. The highest is 100, so the base price is **470.00**.
2. **Apply the discount** (`discount_percent` + `price_order`): 470.00 × (1 − 5 %) = 446.50, so the unit price is **446.50**, rounded half-up to the cent.
3. **Compute the total:** 120 × 446.50 = **53,580.00**.

Output:
```json
{"position": "1", "material_number": "M-4711", "quantity": 120,
 "base_unit_price": 470.00, "unit_price": 446.50, ...}
"total_net": 53580.00
```

### The split in one sentence each
- **Site agents:** "Here are all 3 conditions, exactly as the ERP shows them."
- **Analyst:** "B is the one that applies on the scenario date."
- **Pricing:** "120 pieces reaches the 100 scale, so 470 − 5 % = 446.50, and × 120 = 53,580.00."

In the full challenge, pricing also adds the surcharge, packaging, setup fee and project bonus to the unit price, and checks whether the discount's minimum order value is reached. The structure stays the same: the model chooses which records apply, and the code turns them into numbers.

2	=== [assistant 10-10T19:26:50] Mostly no. I went through the recent runs and the leaderboard. Neither problem is what's costing us points.
3	
4	## What the runs show
5	
6	| Variant | What happened |
7	|---|---|
8	| **cc-agent (Opus)** | Found all the data: 100 in a test run. In the scored run, research finished at 10:51 (about $5). Then the **submission step ran for 9 minutes** and the run timed out at 20:09. |
9	| **lite-agent v1–v5 (Qwen)** | Every run ended with "deadline reached / No evidence". The tender session spent 171s on 8 calls for **one page**, scripting its way past the slider captcha and dumping `innerHTML`. |
10	| **orchestration v2–v5, main** | Quality 5 every time. Each one entered `no_bid` because evidence was incomplete. |
11	
12	The leader (isar-labs) scores 100 in 6:22 for $0.09, which is roughly what Qwen costs. A cheap model is clearly enough.
13	
14	## A different way to look at it
15	
16	**1. Dependencies between tasks are shallow, and already handled.** There are really only two hard ones: Kataloggruppe from the spec before the ERP search, and the TAN arriving after you start signing. Mail also needs the tender reference. sched-agent already orders all of this. More work here won't move the score.
17	
18	**2. Finding where the data is was solved once the model was strong enough.** Opus found everything. With Qwen the problem isn't wrong turns. It's the **cost of each step**: every scroll, gate and paging click is a full model call that reads a big HTML dump, on top of queue wait (main's scored run waited 12 minutes in the queue in total). The actual navigation needs maybe 20–30 decisions; we spend hundreds of calls. The rules let helpers do the mechanical parts: "extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms". Let the model choose; let code do the clicking.
19	
20	**3. The pipeline is all-or-nothing, and that's what our score shows.** We scored 0 or 5 on every run. Scoring gives credit field by field, rule 9 lets you omit positions you didn't finish, and teams ranked 4–10 sit at 10–69 with partial answers. Right now, when evidence is missing we enter `no_bid` (losing everything except the reference) or enter nothing (0). A rough partial bid would already put us in the top 10.
21	
22	**4. The one real click-path problem is the submission form.** It killed the run that would have scored 100. Filling forms is explicitly allowed for helpers: the model maps form fields to answer keys once, and code fills them in and handles the TAN.
23	
24	## What I'd build instead
25	
26	An agent that always has a submittable answer:
27	- **A fact table is the goal.** The resolver runs on every update and always has a best partial bid ready. Missing evidence means omitting that position, never `no_bid`, unless there truly is no matching active material.
28	- **A hard deadline** (around minute 12–13): sign and submit whatever is best at that point.
29	- **Small observations for the model:** numbered links and controls, tables as plain text, no HTML. One model call per real decision. Gates, paging and document extraction are helpers the model calls.
30	- **Submission:** the model maps the form, a helper fills it.
31	
32	Two changes are cheap and worth making first, whatever else we decide:
33	1. Make the resolver fall back to a partial bid instead of `no_bid`.
34	2. Make the submission step helper-driven in cc-agent.
35	
36	On cc-agent's own numbers, research finished at about 11 minutes, so the 9 minutes lost on the form is what pushed it past 20. That's the shortest path to an eligible, high-scoring run. After that, the work is making Qwen fast with smaller observations and helpers.

38	I haven't read through every agent's code yet. Should I start with the resolver fallback and the submission helper?

73	=== [assistant 10-10T19:37:51] Looking for the lite-agent code to confirm what those slow calls are.
74	=== [assistant 10-10T19:43:48] You're right that login is cheap: the Haiku experiment in that thread found each site's login in 16–50 s for under a cent, and code replays it in 2.5–5 s.
75	
76	**The most expensive action on every page is extraction:** the model rewriting the page it just read as JSON (`record_page` in the lite agent). I checked this against all 111 model calls of the last scored run (`run_935ad800d98f6e7f`) and the package it ran.
77	
78	## What the run shows
79	
80	| | Navigation calls (click, navigate, decide) | Extraction calls (`record_page`) |
81	|---|---|---|
82	| Calls | ~95 | **15** |
83	| Typical call | in ~2K / out ~100 tokens, 2–10 s | in ~1.8K / out **5,000–8,500** tokens |
84	| Wall time per call | mostly queue wait (e.g. 4.2 s, of which 3.9 s waiting) | **1.5–4 minutes** |
85	| Share of the 41:39 spent in calls | ~18% | **~82% (~34 min)** |
86	
87	Reading is cheap. **Writing is slow**: Qwen produces about 35 output tokens a second, and most of each extraction's output is thinking. A ~2K-token page turns into 8K tokens of output.
88	
89	## Worse: none of those extractions ever landed
90	
91	In the package, `_record_page` gives each extraction call **60 s** (`llm_agent.py:251`). The calls need 2–4 minutes. So every extraction:
92	1. times out at 60 s;
93	2. is retried with the same input for another 60 s (you can see the pairs: 03:59 and 04:59, 06:50 and 07:50, 09:51 and 10:52);
94	3. fails again, and the agent is told to try again.
95	
96	Each page costs about 2 minutes and records nothing. The tender session ended with "No answer; gaps: Record every position of the bill of quantities". It had found the bill of quantities but never managed to write it down.
97	
98	Claude Code has the same problem at a smaller scale. The other thread measured the 100 run's final 24K-token evidence JSON at about 3 minutes.
99	
100	## What follows
101	
102	Navigation isn't the expensive part; the model copying data out by hand is. Fixes, roughly in order of effort:
103	
104	1. **Turn off thinking for extraction calls.** The other thread was about to test whether the proxy allows that, but I couldn't find a result recorded yet. That alone could cut output from ~8K to ~1–2K tokens.
105	2. **Make the timeout fit the call, or cap the output.** Right now we pay for calls we then throw away. The server keeps generating after we give up.
106	3. **Don't make the model copy values at all.** Code turns the page's tables and lists into rows (the rules allow helpers to "extract a selected page, parse a selected document"). The model only says which table matters and what its columns mean, which is tens of output tokens instead of thousands. The values are then copied exactly instead of transcribed.
107	
108	Option 3 is the real fix, and it matters most on the ERP and Q&A pages, where the tables are biggest. Want me to try 1 and 2 on the lite agent first? They're quick, and would show within one run whether extraction lands at all.
109	=== [user 10-10T19:45:42] How could we make this little helpers idempotent, like regardless of browser state always the katalog is retrieved
110	=== [assistant 10-10T19:46:28] Make each helper **goal-based**: it doesn't replay steps from wherever the browser happens to be. It checks whether the result is already there, brings the page back to a known state if not, carries out the action, and checks the result before returning. If two calls with the same group always get the same rows, the helper is idempotent.
111	
112	## The pattern: check, recover, act, verify
113	
114	```python
115	async def erp_catalog(group: str) -> Rows:
116	    if hit := cache.get(("erp", group)):              # 1. done already → same answer
117	        return hit
118	    page = await ctx.new_page()                        # 2. own tab: no leftover popups or old searches
119	    try:
120	        for _ in range(8):                             # 3. step toward the goal, with a cap
121	            state = await classify(page)               #    cheap DOM checks, not a model call
122	            if state == "result" and await shows_query(page, group):
123	                rows = await read_all_pages(page)      # 4. paginate to the end, dedupe by material no.
124	                if verify(rows, group):                # 5. check the result really answers this query
125	                    cache[("erp", group)] = rows
126	                    return rows
127	            await HANDLERS[state](page, group)         #    logged out → relogin, popup → close, 503 → retry,
128	                                                       #    gate → small model call, other → go to the entry point
129	        raise NeedsModel(state, await screenshot(page))   # 6. escalate, never guess
130	    finally:
131	        await page.close()
132	```
133	
134	What makes it idempotent:
135	
136	1. **Check the result first.** The first thing a call does is see whether the result is already there (cache, or the page already showing that group's results). Calling it twice changes nothing.
137	2. **A fresh tab every call.** A new page in the same browser context shares the login cookies but none of the UI state, so old searches, open F4 popups and half-filled fields can't leak in. Close it afterwards.
138	3. **Bring the page back to a known start, then act.** Never trust where the browser is; go back to a known point first. In order of robustness:
139	   - **Replay the network request.** When the model makes its first search, capture the HTTP request it triggers (`page.on("request")`). If the search is a GET or a simple POST, replay it with `fetch()` in the logged-in page, swapping in the group. No DOM state is involved at all; that's the most robust option.
140	   - **Deep link.** If the result page has a URL with the query in it (`?q=…`), go there directly.
141	   - **Reset command.** SAP-style systems have one built in: `/n<transaction code>` jumps to a fresh screen from anywhere.
142	   - **Replay the UI steps** from the entry URL, using the role and label steps Playwright MCP already reports (as in the login experiment). Use this only as a last resort.
143	4. **Check against the query, not just "a table is visible".** The classic idempotency bug is reading the *previous* search's table before the new one has loaded. Before accepting rows, check that the result shows *this* query: the search field contains the group, or every row carries that Kataloggruppe, or the table has changed since before the search. Also check: at most 20 rows, otherwise the search was too broad (rule 10), and zero rows means the search failed, not "no materials".
144	5. **One handler per state, each idempotent itself.**
145	   - **Relogin:** uses the recorded login. One lock per site, so two tabs never log in at once (the ERP returns 403 for that).
146	   - **Close popup:** closing something already closed does nothing.
147	   - **503 page:** reload with backoff.
148	   - **Session expired:** relogin, then start the loop over.
149	   - **Gate** (receipt number in an image, robot check): a small model call with a screenshot, not code, per the earlier fair-play reasoning.
150	6. **A step cap, then hand back to the model.** After 8 rounds the helper raises with the state and a screenshot. The research agent takes over with raw browser tools.
151	
152	## Where the site knowledge comes from (fair play, and the private dataset)
153	
154	None of this can be written into the package for public-1. Each run **learns it** from the model's first manual search:
155	
156	1. The ERP agent searches for the first Kataloggruppe step by step, as today.
157	2. Code records three things: the network request, the UI steps, and how the model recognized a correct result.
158	3. These become the routine for this run. **The first replay is checked against the model's own manual result** (same rows?) before anyone relies on it.
159	4. For every further group: `erp_catalog(group)` is one tool call, and the model still chooses which groups (rule 11 allows helpers to "paginate a model-selected result set").
160	
161	The state checks (`classify`) are generic: a password field means logged out, a known overlay button means popup, an HTTP status or "Erneut versuchen" means retry. Only "this is the result page" comes from what was learned in the run.
162	
163	## What I'd check first
164	
165	One look decides which recovery method to use: when you search for a Kataloggruppe in the ERP, what request goes out? A plain GET, or a form post with a session token, or an SAP-style stateful screen flow? I couldn't find any recorded ERP URLs in our logs or local outputs. The quickest way is the scouting login in a browser with DevTools open.
166	
167	- **Plain request:** network replay makes the helper nearly bulletproof.
168	- **Stateful flow:** we need the reset-command or UI-replay route, and the check against the query matters even more.
169	
170	Should I check that, or prototype `erp_catalog` with the loop above in sched-agent?
171	=== [user 10-10T19:47:17] maybe we always start with login front page as the common ground
172	=== [assistant 10-10T19:47:26] Yes, that's a good simplification, with one refinement: use the **home page after login** as the common starting point, not the login page itself. You go to the start URL every time, but you only log in when the site actually asks.
173	
174	## Why not log in on every call
175	
176	- **The ERP login includes a gate.** The receipt number changes every time and is only shown as an image, so every login needs a model call. Ten catalog searches would mean ten gate calls.
177	- **Parallel logins break each other.** The ERP returned 403 when two tabs logged in at once. Some sites also end the old session on a new login, which would kill the other helpers' tabs mid-search.
178	- **Time.** A replayed login takes 2.5–5 s, and the ERP's more because of the gate. Opening the start URL while logged in takes about 1 s.
179	
180	## The refined version
181	
182	```python
183	async def erp_catalog(group):
184	    page = await ctx.new_page()                       # fresh tab, shared cookies
185	    await page.goto(START_URL)                        # the common starting point, every call
186	    if await looks_logged_out(page):                  # password field visible
187	        async with login_lock["erp"]:                 # only one login at a time per site
188	            await relogin(page)                       # recorded steps; gate → small model call
189	    await dismiss_overlays(page)
190	    await replay(path_from_home, group=group)         # learned in this run, from home to the result
191	    rows = await read_all_pages(page)
192	    assert shows_query(page, group) and 0 < len(rows) <= 20
193	    return rows
194	```
195	
196	What you get:
197	- **Every call starts from the same place,** so you only need **one** recorded path (home → result), not a recovery plan for every possible state.
198	- **Login only when the session is really gone** (ERP's short timeout), and never two at once.
199	- **The leftover-state problem disappears:** a fresh tab plus a fresh start means no old searches and no open popups.
200	
201	It costs about 1–2 s extra per call for the trip back home. That's nothing next to a model call.
202	
203	## What to watch for
204	
205	- **Some sites send you back to where you were** instead of showing home after a fresh `goto`. Check that the page really looks like home; if not, use a logout link or the SAP-style reset (`/n…`).
206	- **Gates that come back mid-session** (the mail gate after new messages) aren't fixed by going home. They stay a handler: detect, short model call, continue.
207	- **Still check the result:** going home fixes the start but not a result table that loads late. The `shows_query` check against the group stays.
208	
209	So: same start every time, log in only when needed, one recorded path, check the result. Want me to build it as `erp_catalog` in sched-agent and run it locally with the scouting login, calling it twice in a row and once after a deliberately expired session?
210	=== [user 10-10T19:48:25] What are all the different actions we need based on the generic task description
211	=== [assistant 10-10T19:48:45] I went through the brief and its 29 rules. Leaving public-1's layout aside, everything breaks down into about **20 generic actions** in four groups, plus a list of **which facts to fetch** that the model works through using those actions.
212	
213	## 1. Session actions (every site, run by code)
214	
215	| Action | What it does | Idempotent because |
216	|---|---|---|
217	| `go_home(site)` | fresh tab, open the start URL | always the same start |
218	| `login(site)` | recorded login, one at a time per site | only runs when a password field is visible |
219	| `dismiss_overlays()` | cookie walls, survey popups, banners, dialogs | closing something already closed does nothing |
220	| `retry_error()` | flaky/503 pages: reload with backoff | stops once the page is fine |
221	| `pass_gate()` | slider, "not a robot", code shown in an image: **small model call** | only runs when a gate is detected |
222	
223	## 2. Reading actions (generic, the model chooses the target)
224	
225	| Action | Needed for (rule) |
226	|---|---|
227	| `read(page)` → compact text plus tables as rows, including tooltips and collapsed sections | everything |
228	| `links()` / `open(link)` | the model's choice of the next step |
229	| `search(query)` → result list, rejected if empty or more than 20 hits | ERP by Kataloggruppe (10), mail by reference + topic (10) |
230	| `all_pages(list)` → page through / "load more" to the end, dedupe | Q&A, requirement tables, mail results, ERP results |
231	| `open_items(list, ids)` → open selected detail pages, including their tabs | materials, messages, Q&A answers |
232	| `open_frame()` | nested document viewers, iframes |
233	| `download_parse(link)` → ZIP, PDF, text | tender documents |
234	| `switch_folder(name)` | mail: inbox ↔ archive |
235	
236	## 3. Writing actions (change state, so check before acting)
237	
238	| Action | Check first |
239	|---|---|
240	| `express_interest(tender)` (unlocks documents) | already unlocked? |
241	| `fill_bid(answer)`: the model maps form labels to answer keys once, code fills; positions can be omitted (9) | form already holds these values? |
242	| `request_signing()` | was a TAN requested after the bid was saved? |
243	| `wait_for_tan(after=t)`: newest TAN message after the request time | ignore older TANs |
244	| `enter_tan_and_submit()` → read the confirmation | already submitted? |
245	
246	## 4. Computing (code, no browser)
247	
248	`resolve(evidence)`: rules 1–8 and 12–28 (quantity, revision, material, price scales, FX, discount, packaging, setup pool, bonus, delivery, totals). This already exists in `bid_engine/resolver.py`.
249	
250	## Which facts the model has to fetch with these actions
251	
252	Grouped by **type of source**, because on the private dataset they may be split across websites differently:
253	
254	| Source | Facts | Rules |
255	|---|---|---|
256	| **Tender** | reference, deadline + timezone, scenario date; positions with quantity and **unit** (Satz) | 1, 17, 21 |
257	| **Tender Q&A** (every answer) | quantity changes, **withdrawals**, technical amendments (revision + requirement + attributes), keys: Konditionsgruppe, packaging tariff, delivery commitment, setup pool, project bonus membership | 1, 12–14, 23–26 |
258	| **Specification** | all revisions plus **which is marked current**; per requirement: bore, stroke, pressure, mounting, certification, **Kataloggruppe**, pieces per set, "nutzbarer Weg" | 2, 17, 20 |
259	| **ERP**, per Kataloggruppe | candidates with status and attributes; per candidate: price conditions (validity, scales, currency, FX key, price unit), stock, lead times stock/production, carton size, allocation mass, surcharge mass / metal basis, setup fee | 3, 4, 6, 15, 22–25 |
260	| **Mail**, reference + topic, inbox **and** archive | director discount approval (+ threshold), Konditionsregeln, Technikfreigabe, Verpackungstarife, Terminfreigabe, Devisenfixing, Rüstpools, Projektbonus, Preisindizes, each with sender, date and reference; plus your own mail domain, and later the TAN | 5, 12, 16, 20–28 |
261	
262	## What follows
263	
264	- **About 20 actions cover the whole task.** Only `pass_gate`, the choice of target, and form mapping need the model. Everything else is code. Isar-labs must be working with roughly this.
265	- **The facts table is the checklist:** the model works through it. "Missing" means it fetches more, and anything still missing at the deadline means omitting that position (no `no_bid`).

267	- **The writing actions are where it's riskiest.** They change state, so they need the "check first" from the table, otherwise a retry submits twice or reads an old TAN.
268	
269	Should I put this in a file (e.g. `docs/actions.md`) as the basis for the helpers, and then start with `search` + `all_pages` + `open_items` for the ERP?
270	=== [user 10-10T19:57:00] should we decide which actions we need ad hoc or can we hardcode all of those actions for agents to find out?
271	=== [assistant 10-10T19:57:19] Do both, at different levels. **Hardcode the verbs** (the ~20 generic actions). **Learn the bindings at run time:** where on this particular website each verb applies, plus a fallback for anything no verb covers.
272	
273	## Why the verbs can be hardcoded
274	
275	The actions come from the **task**, not the websites. The brief promises the private dataset has "the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format". What changes is the software, layout, navigation and how the information is split up. So there will be search, paged lists, documents, a mailbox and a form on the private sites too, just elsewhere and looking different.
276	
277	Having agents invent the actions afresh each run would be slower, more expensive and less reliable, especially for Qwen. That's exactly the model turns we want to get rid of.
278	
279	The fair-play line also runs right there:
280	- ✅ **Generic verbs on targets the model chooses** (`search(query)`, `all_pages(list)`, `open_items(ids)`, `fill(form)`) are explicitly allowed.
281	- ❌ **Site-specific paths** (URLs, selectors, click sequences from public-1) in the package are rejected, and would break on the private dataset anyway.
282	- ❌ **A verb that collects everything on its own** (`crawl_site()`) is rejected too.
283	
284	## Three levels
285	
286	| Level | What | Where it comes from |
287	|---|---|---|
288	| **1. Verbs** | `go_home`, `login`, `dismiss_overlays`, `search`, `all_pages`, `open_items`, `read`, `download_parse`, `fill_bid`, `wait_for_tan`, …, each with "check first" and "check the result" built in | **hardcoded** in the package |
289	| **2. Bindings** | where on **this** website: start URL, login steps, which field is the search box, which control is "next page", how a result row looks, the network request behind a search | **learned in the run:** the model points once, code records and replays it |
290	| **3. Fallback** | raw `click` / `type` / `snapshot` / `evaluate` | for anything no verb fits |
291	
292	## How a binding is learned (one model decision instead of a script)
293	
294	```
295	first search(group) on the ERP: binding unknown
296	  → code shows the model a compact element list
297	  → model: "the search field is [e12], results are in table [t3], next page is [e40]"
298	  → code records them by role and name (plus the network request), runs the search, checks the result
299	every further search(group): binding known → no model call, just code
300	binding fails (layout changed, session expired) → go home, try again → still failing: ask the model again
301	```
302	
303	The model only **points**, it doesn't write code. That's a choice of a few tokens, which Qwen can make reliably and quickly.
304	
305	## What we hardcode besides the verbs, and what we don't
306	
307	- **Hardcode:** the facts checklist (evidence schema) and the resolver. Both come from the rules, which stay the same.
308	- **Don't hardcode:** the order of sites, how the information is split, which site holds what. The model decides that from the checklist and what it observes. If the private dataset has the Q&A in the mail instead of the tender portal, only the binding changes, not the verb.
309	
310	## How we find missing verbs
311	
312	**Log every time the fallback is used.** If the model regularly falls back to raw clicks for the same kind of thing (e.g. an infinite scroll list, or a calendar picker), that's a missing verb. Test on varied sites, not just public-1. That way the verb set grows from evidence, not guesswork.

314	So: fixed verbs, learned bindings, a raw fallback. That's flexible enough for unfamiliar websites and still saves most of the model turns.

316	=== [assistant 10-10T19:59:54] It's the most important building block, but not enough on its own. `go_home` + `login` gives every action the **same starting point**. Idempotent means the action also gets the **same result** and **doesn't do anything twice**, and that needs three more things.
317	
318	## What go_home + login solves
319	
320	- the browser is somewhere unknown (other page, old search, half-filled form)
321	- the session expired
322	- leftover popups and dialogs (if you also open a fresh tab)
323	
324	## What it doesn't solve
325	
326	| Problem | Example | What's needed in addition |
327	|---|---|---|
328	| **Stale result** | the result table from the previous search is still showing while the new one loads, and gets read as the answer | **check the result against the query:** the search field contains this group, the rows carry this Kataloggruppe, at most 20 hits |
329	| **Incomplete reading** | only page 1 of 3, or "load more" not clicked | **read to the end:** until there's no "next", deduplicated by ID |
330	| **Gates in the middle** | the mail gate appears again after new messages, even when logged in | **handler:** detect the gate, short model call, carry on |
331	| **Writing twice** | a retry expresses interest twice, saves a second bid, or takes an old TAN | **check before writing:** already unlocked? bid already there? TAN newer than the signing request? |
332	
333	## So per action
334	
335	```
336	go_home + login if needed  →  dismiss overlays  →  path from home (binding)
337	→  do it  →  check the result against the query  →  read to the end
338	(writing actions: check first whether it's already done)
339	```
340	
341	The first part is the same for every action and exists once. The **result check** is short, but has to be written per verb. Without it, the same call can return different answers, which is the worst case because it fails silently.
342	
343	**In short:** go_home + login is the common starting point, and the result check is what makes an action really idempotent. Both together are only a few lines per verb.

1	=== [user 10-10T19:39:09] look at .t3 thread id 9939e89c-45cb-40b6-b613-8ed6c3d4e783
2	
3	how would a custom harness look like? Like opening a page and then dumping the page to model context and saying the model it should format the tool calls for login?
4	=== [assistant 10-10T19:39:32] I'm reading the end of that thread to see where the harness discussion landed, then I'll answer.
5	=== [assistant 10-10T19:39:36] The thread already started a Qwen custom harness at `orchestrated/login_qwen.py`. I'm reading it so I can answer with the concrete design.
6	=== [assistant 10-10T19:39:51] Mostly yes, with one important difference. The model doesn't get the page once and then write out the whole login. It runs in a **loop, one action per turn**, and it sees the new page after every action. The thread built exactly this before it stopped, in `orchestrated/login_qwen.py` (187 lines).
7	
8	## How it works
9	
10	```
11	messages = [system prompt (~10 lines), "site X, url, user, pw. Start with goto."]
12	loop up to 30 turns:
13	    reply = qwen.chat(messages, tools=7 small tools, thinking off)
14	    for each tool call in reply:
15	        done(marker)      → stop
16	        otherwise         → harness runs it with Playwright
17	                            record it as a script step (credentials → {username}/{password})
18	                            result = new page as an accessibility tree (≤5,000 chars)
19	                            or "Error: ..." + the page, so the model can try something else
20	    shorten older page results to 300 chars
21	replay(script) in a fresh browser, no model  → did it work?
22	```
23	
24	Three details matter:
25	
26	1. **The model doesn't format the tool calls in text.** The harness passes JSON schemas in the API's `tools` parameter (`goto`, `fill`, `click`, `press`, `check`, `slider_max`, `done`). Qwen returns structured `tool_calls` that the harness reads directly, so there's no text to parse.
27	2. **The page isn't sent as HTML.** It's sent as Playwright's `aria_snapshot()`, lines like `- textbox "Benutzername"` and `- button "Anmelden"`. That's a fraction of the size of the HTML, and the model can name elements with it directly: `click(role="button", name="Anmelden")` becomes `page.get_by_role("button", name="Anmelden")`.
28	3. **The loop is what makes it adaptive.** A page dump plus "write the login steps" can't work, because the model can't see what comes after the first click: the cookie wall, the ERP's 503 page, the slider, the receipt number. That approach would also come close to the "crawl-then-one-shot" pattern that Atira's fair-play rules reject. In the loop design, the model decides each step from what it actually sees.
29	
30	## Why it's cheaper than Claude Code
31	
32	| | Claude Code + Playwright MCP | Custom harness |
33	|---|---|---|
34	| Fixed prompt per call | ~30–40K tokens (system prompt and about 20 MCP tool schemas) | ~300 tokens and 7 tiny tools |
35	| Old pages | stay in context in full | cut to 300 chars, only the latest page is kept whole |
36	| Thinking | model default | turned off (`enable_thinking: False`) |
37	| Recording | parsed out of the log afterwards | built in: every step that works becomes a replayable script step |
38	
39	The cost is that you write the loop, the tools and the error handling yourself. For a narrow job like logging in, that's under 200 lines. For open-ended research across four sites, Claude Code's general features earn their overhead more often.
40	
41	## Run status
42	
43	The Qwen run the thread started at 21:36 (`out/login-qwen-20261010-213620/`) hasn't written its `results.json`. It's either still running or it crashed after the parameter-name fix, so there are no Qwen numbers yet to put next to Haiku's ($0.028 total, 16–50 s per site). I didn't rerun it. It needs `atira models proxy` running; then:
44	
45	```
46	my-agent/.venv/bin/python orchestrated/login_qwen.py
47	```
48	
49	It prints the same table as the Haiku experiment, so the two can be compared directly.
50	=== [user 10-10T19:40:41] so its like the accessibility tree
51	=== [assistant 10-10T19:40:47] Yes. What the model sees after each action is the page's **accessibility tree**: the version of the page a screen reader gets. Each element is reduced to its role (button, textbox, link, heading, checkbox, slider) and its accessible name. Layout, CSS, scripts and most of the markup are dropped.
52	
53	For a login page, the call in `login_qwen.py:64` (`page.locator("body").aria_snapshot()`) returns roughly this:
54	
55	```
56	URL: https://…/login
57	Title: Anmeldung
58	- heading "Anmelden" [level=1]
59	- textbox "Benutzername"
60	- textbox "Passwort"
61	- checkbox "Angemeldet bleiben"
62	- button "Anmelden"
63	- dialog "Cookies":
64	  - button "Notwendige Cookies akzeptieren"
65	```
66	
67	**Why it fits this job:**
68	- **It's small.** A login page is a few hundred characters instead of tens of KB of HTML.
69	- **The model can act on it directly.** It answers `click(role="button", name="Anmelden")`, and the harness passes that straight to `page.get_by_role(...)`. No CSS selectors or coordinates are involved.
70	- **The steps hold up on replay.** Role plus name usually stays the same between page loads, which is why the recorded script can run again in a fresh browser.
71	
72	**Claude Code uses it too.** Playwright MCP's `browser_snapshot` returns the same kind of tree, with refs like `[ref=e12]` added. So the custom harness doesn't see the page differently. It saves by sending far less around the tree: a short prompt, 7 tools instead of about 20, and old pages shortened.
73	
74	**Where it stops working:**
75	- **Anything shown only as an image or canvas.** The ERP's receipt number is an example. It isn't in the tree, which is why that step was marked `model_needed`. Reading it needs a screenshot and a model that can see images.
76	- **Elements without a proper name**, such as an icon button with no label. The tree shows just `- button`, and the model can't tell those buttons apart.
77	- **Long pages.** The harness cuts each snapshot at 5,000 characters (`OBSERVATION_CHARS`), so on big ERP lists the button the model needs can be cut off. That's fine for logins, but it would need scrolling or a search for research pages.
