80	=== [assistant 10-10T19:42:19] Yes, that's the right structure. I'd make each fallback a **tool**, and have the system prompt say only when to reach for it. A short prompt is enough because the tool descriptions carry the detail.
81	
82	I checked the image question first: Atira's hosted Qwen accepts images through the proxy. In a one-image test it correctly read a word off a screenshot. So the fallback can be the same model looking at a screenshot, with no second provider. I only checked that it reads text from an image, not how well it handles noisy, CAPTCHA-style digits.
83	
84	## The order of fallbacks
85	
86	| Step | Tool | When | Cost |
87	|---|---|---|---|
88	| 1 | *(none, automatic)* | After every action the model gets the accessibility tree | small, text only |
89	| 2 | `find(text)` | The tree was cut at 5,000 chars and the element isn't in the visible part | small |
90	| 3 | `screenshot()` | Something is shown only as an image (a code, a receipt number), buttons have no names, or the tree is empty | an image, several times more tokens |
91	| 4 | `click_at(x, y)` | An element visible in the screenshot can't be addressed by role and name | small |
92	| 5 | `give_up(reason)` | Stuck after a few tries | ends the session, saves turns |
93	
94	## Proposed system prompt
95	
96	```
97	You log in to one website in a browser. It is a fictional demo system built for an
98	agent challenge; cookie walls, error pages and check gates (sliders, "I'm not a
99	robot", codes to retype) are deliberate obstacles you are expected to pass.
100	
101	After each action you see the page as an accessibility tree: lines like
102	`- textbox "Benutzername"` or `- button "Anmelden"`. Address elements by that role
103	and name. This is your main view; use it whenever it shows what you need.
104	
105	If the tree is not enough:
106	- The element you expect is missing and the tree says it was cut → find(text).
107	- Information is only visible as an image, buttons have no names, or the tree is
108	  empty or makes no sense → screenshot(). Then act by role/name if you can,
109	  otherwise click_at(x, y).
110	- An action fails twice the same way → try a different approach, not the same call.
111	- After 3 different approaches without progress → give_up with what blocks you.
112	
113	Call exactly one tool per turn. If you type a value that is read from the page and
114	changes every time (not the username or password), set changes_each_time.
115	When the page behind the login is shown, call done with a text that is only visible
116	when logged in. Do nothing beyond logging in.
117	```
118	
119	## Two things I'd also do in the harness, not in the prompt
120	
121	- **Automatic escalation.** A small model like Qwen Flash doesn't reliably notice when it's stuck. So the harness should add a screenshot to the observation on its own when the tree is empty, the URL hasn't changed for 3 actions, or the same error comes back twice. The prompt rule is the first line of defence; the harness rule makes sure escalation actually happens.
122	- **Recording.** `find` and `screenshot` don't change the page, so they shouldn't become script steps. `click_at` becomes a step only with a warning flag, because coordinates break at other window sizes. A value read from a screenshot is always saved as `model_needed`, like the ERP's receipt number.
123

35	
36	1. **The model chooses, code acts.** Stagehand (Browserbase) is built on this. A point is about 30 tokens, where Haiku writing Playwright code was 1,000–4,000.
37	
38	2. **Learn a step once, then replay it as code.** This is the biggest documented saving:
39	   - Skyvern turns a successful run into Playwright code and replays it without a model. It reports about 70–90% fewer tokens.
40	   - browser-use's workflow-use records a run as a workflow with variables and claims 10× faster and about 90% cheaper.
41	   - Stagehand caches resolved actions and checks each cache hit against a hash of the page's structure.
42	
43	   These figures are the vendors' own.
44	
45	3. **Replay breaks, and every tool has to handle it.** Each tool checks the page before using a recorded step and lets the model take over again when the check fails. workflow-use's replay was once completely broken by a browser-use update. We hit the same thing: the ERP replay failed all three times once the waits were removed, and two replays failed on a check text the model invented. Before each recorded step, check that the element is visible and ready. After it, check that the expected text is actually on the page. If either check fails, hand the step back to the model.

47	4. **Extraction is a separate step with a schema.** Stagehand's `extract` and browser-use's extract action turn the page into text with code first. 51	## What applies to us, and what doesn't
52	
53	The vendors' big savings come from the **cache carried between runs**. We can't use that: fair play forbids putting site-specific steps in the package, so each run starts from zero. That leaves three levers:
54	
55	| Lever | Our case | Expected effect |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| Point, don't write | every page decision | the largest: output drops from ~1–4K tokens to ~30, and with it most of the time |
58	| Code extraction with a schema | ERP materials, tender items, mails | removes the 3–4 minute Qwen calls |
59	| Replay within one run | repeated ERP searches, re-logins, the submission form | real gains, because these repeat |

75	=== [assistant 10-10T20:14:08] Yes. With fixed code that presents numbered options, Clef fits much better than when the timeout thread set it aside at 18:52. Its objection then was that Clef only saves time "where code drives the browser and a model only has to choose", which is now exactly the design.
76	
77	I ran one quick test through the local proxy. I gave it a login page as a numbered element list and asked three questions in one call:
78	
79	| Question | Clef's answer | Confidence |
80	|---|---|---|
81	| Which element takes the username? | `e3` textbox "Benutzername" | 0.97 |
82	| Which element submits the login? | `e6` button "Anmelden" | 0.92 |
83	| Is a cookie banner blocking the page? (yes/no) | 0.89 yes | |
84	
85	- **Speed:** 0.8–2.5 s per call, with all three answers in that one call. The same answers came back all three times.
86	- **Cost:** 745 input tokens, about $0.0002. Output isn't charged.
87	- **Confidence:** every answer comes with a probability for each option. Code can use that to decide when to escalate: accept anything above about 0.8, and send the rest to Qwen.
88	
89	## How the work would split
90	
91	| Clef: choose and check | Qwen: produce text |
92	|---|---|
93	| which element is the search field, results table or next-page link | what to search for ("GR-5152") |
94	| which links or result rows to open | values to type into fields |
95	| which column holds freely available stock | reading a receipt number from an image |
96	| yes/no checks: is this the right document? is this mail about this tender? is a gate showing? did the login work? | rare free-form steps where no option fits |
97	
98	Mapping columns is also just a choice. Combined with code that pulls the table out, much of the extraction then needs no model writing at all, which is where the 3–4 minute Qwen calls came from.
99	
100	The fair-play risk is low: the brief itself suggests Clef for "which link to open or whether a page is the right document". The model still makes every navigation decision, so it isn't a fixed script.
101	
102	## What I haven't tested
103	
104	- **Real pages.** This page was synthetic, short and easy. A list of 100+ links on a real page, or very similar options like several "Weiter" buttons, could do worse.
105	- **Cold start.** An idle Clef can take minutes to wake up. That isn't counted toward a submission's time, but `agent.json` has to list `"clef"` under `models` so the run waits for it.
106	- **Limits:** 16 calls at once per team, and Clef can't produce any text.
107	
108	The timeout thread is building the pointing prototype in `orchestrated/point.py` right now. 109	=== [user 10-10T20:18:40] I mean lets think about it so look at .t3 thread id 9939e89c-45cb-40b6-b613-8ed6c3d4e783 how do we reliably figure out when login succeeds? or things like this so what should the model and what should the harness do
110	=== [assistant 10-10T20:19:13] The pattern in that thread is that both ways of deciding "did it work" have failed so far:
111	
112	- **The model chose the check:** Haiku and Qwen both named check texts that weren't on the page, so two replays failed although the login had worked.
113	- **The harness used a rule that only fit some sites:** "no password field and no slider" marked the webmail as logged out, because it shows a slider in the reading pane.
114	- **Nobody tracked progress:** Qwen dragged the ERP slider about 12 times in a loop, and nothing noticed the page wasn't changing.
115	
116	The fix is a simple rule: **the model proposes, the harness verifies.** The harness checks every fact that code can check. The model judges only what code can't, and only by choosing from things the harness has confirmed exist on the page.
117	
118	## Login success
119	
120	**1. Detect the login form, not success.** Code can reliably spot a visible password field. That gives one generic check:
121	- the password field is gone after submitting, and
122	- after reloading the site's start URL, it's still gone, meaning the site doesn't send you back to the login page.
123	
124	Then you're logged in. That's true on any site, and it doesn't care what else is on the page, like the webmail's slider.
125	
126	**2. Gather more signals in code, all generic:**
127	
128	| Signal | Means |
129	|---|---|
130	| a logout control appears ("Abmelden", "Logout", "Sign out" …) | strong yes |
131	| the login form is still there, plus an error text or `role=alert` | clear no |
132	| the URL left the login path, a new session cookie was set | weak yes |
133	| a gate element appeared (slider, checkbox, image code) | not done yet: a gate, not a failure |
134	
135	If all signals agree, code decides with no model call.
136	
137	**3. The model only resolves unclear cases.** Code gives it the elements that appeared and disappeared since the click. It asks one yes/no question, "Does this show a logged-in area?", for example with Clef (about 1 s, $0.0002).
138	
139	**4. Never let the model make up the check text.** Code computes which texts are new on the page after login, and the model picks one from that list. A logout control is chosen automatically if there is one. The check text is then guaranteed to exist, which removes the cause of both failed replays.
140	
141	**5. Session timeouts come for free.** The same password-field check run before every action notices when a session has expired. The harness then replays the recorded login in 2–5 s.
142	
143	## The same pattern for every step
144	
145	After every action, the harness sorts the result into one of a few outcomes and tells the model in one line, instead of sending it the whole page:
146	
147	```
148	after each action:
149	  wait until the page stops changing (element list stable, no pending navigation)
150	  diff = elements before vs after   (main page, frames, popup windows)
151	  outcome =
152	    error     if error text, role=alert, an HTTP 4xx/5xx page
153	    gate      if slider / robot checkbox / image code appeared
154	    no effect if the page is unchanged
155	    loop      if this page state was already seen in this task
156	    progress  otherwise
157	  → model sees: "clicked 'Weiter' → no effect (3rd time on this page state)"
158	```
159	
160	- **No effect** and **loop** fix the Qwen problem directly. The harness keeps a hash of each page state and notices when one repeats. It then forbids the last action and tells the model to try something else.
161	- **Error** is handled by code where it's generic (reloading a 503 page, retrying). Otherwise the model gets one line explaining it.
162	- **Recording:** each step is saved with its action and the outcome it produced, for example "Anmelden → login form gone, 'Abmelden' present". On replay, a step whose expected outcome doesn't appear is handed back to the model instead of failing silently. That's the exact gap the workflow-use developers call "currently really bad".
163	
164	## Who does what
165	
166	| Harness (generic code) | Model |
167	|---|---|
168	| list the elements, including frames and popup windows | which element serves the goal |
169	| act, wait until the page is stable, compare before and after | what to type: search terms, values |
170	| sort each result: progress / no effect / error / gate / loop | unclear results ("is this the right area? the right document?") |
171	| login check via password field and reload; re-login on timeout | choose a check text from the ones that verifiably exist |
172	| detect loops and block repeats | another approach once a loop is reported |
173	| record steps with their expected outcome; replay and check it | read text in images (receipt number); decisions at gates |
174	| deadlines and timeouts | — |
175	
176	Clef fits the right column wherever the answer is "pick one of these" or yes/no. Qwen handles anything that has to produce text.
177	
178	None of this is tied to public-1 sites: password fields, alerts, unchanged pages and repeated states look the same on any website. The rules for detecting gates are the most heuristic part and will need testing on other pages.
179	
180	The timeout thread has meanwhile started testing Browser Use itself with Qwen. Its findings on how Browser Use judges success (its per-step self-evaluation) are worth comparing with this before building more.

182	=== [assistant 10-10T20:21:07] You're right that the login answer doesn't scale on its own. The good news is that the 20 verbs don't need 20 checks. Looking at the list in `orchestrated/verbs.py`, they come in **four shapes**, and each shape has one generic way to check success. On top of that comes one check after every single action, the same for every verb.
183	
184	## The four shapes
185	
186	| Shape | Verbs | Success means | How code checks it |
187	|---|---|---|---|
188	| **Open one specific thing** | `find_tender`, the first step of `read_material` and `read_message` | the page is about *this* item, not a look-alike | the parameter (reference, material number) appears **exactly** in the page's heading or a key field; `VG-2027-7093-A` doesn't count for `VG-2027-7093` |
189	| **Read a list completely** | `read_boq`, `read_qa`, `list_documents`, `list_spec_documents`, `list_revisions`, `read_requirements`, `search_catalog`, `search_mail` | every row, every page | the "next" control is gone or disabled; a shown total ("1–20 von 47") matches the rows read; no duplicate rows; rows match the filter (e.g. the Kataloggruppe searched for) |
190	| **Read one record** | `read_material`, `read_message`, `read_document`, `inspect_bid_form` | all its fields, from all tabs | the identity check above, plus: all tabs or sections visited, and the result schema's required fields are filled |
191	| **Change something** | `login`, `express_interest`, filling and signing the bid | the change stuck | **reload and read it again**: the new state is still there. That's the login check made general: "password field still gone after reload" is the login case of "state persists after reload" |
192	
193	Each verb then only declares which shape it is, its result schema and its identity parameter. That's one line per verb, all generic, nothing site-specific.
194	
195	## The check after every action (all verbs)
196	
197	Code sorts every click or input the same way, whatever the verb:
198	- **progress**
199	- **no effect:** the page didn't change
200	- **error:** error text, an alert, a 4xx/5xx page
201	- **gate:** a slider, robot checkbox or image code appeared
202	- **logged out:** the password field is back, so code runs the recorded login and repeats the step
203	- **loop:** this page state was already seen in this task
204	
205	This step-by-step check catches problems along the way. The shape check decides whether the verb as a whole succeeded.
206	
207	## Who does what
208	
209	**The harness checks everything it can measure:**
210	- exact identity matches
211	- whether paging is exhausted, and whether the count matches the shown total
212	- whether the result fits the schema
213	- whether a change survives a reload
214	- the outcome of each action, including loops
215	
216	**The model handles the meaning:**
217	- **Pointing**, when code can't find something by itself: "which element shows the total?", "which control is next page?", "which field is the reference?". These are choices among elements that exist, so Clef fits.
218	- **Judging look-alikes and status** when the exact match is unclear: "Is this the current revision or a superseded one?", "Is this mail about this tender?"
219	- **Deciding what to do** after a failed check: try another path, or report that it can't be done.
220	
221	## The final check: the resolver
222	
223	Every verb exists to fill the fact table, and `bid_engine` knows which fields it needs. So the true end-to-end check is whether the resolver has everything it needs for a bid. A verb whose result leaves a field the resolver needs empty has failed, whatever its own checks said. `missing_keys` in `my-agent/llm_agent.py` already does a simple version of this.
224	
225	## Where it stays hard
226	
227	- **Completeness without a shown total.** If a list shows neither "x of N" nor a page count, code can only see that the "next" control disappeared. Infinite scrolling or "load more" needs the model to point once at what loads more.
228	- **Exact matching depends on how the site writes things.** Spaces, hyphens and leading zeros differ between sites. Code has to normalize them, and the model decides the leftover look-alikes.
229	
230	So there are four checks plus one per-action check, not 20. The verbs themselves can still be learned per site, as `verbs.py` does now. Each shape's check also gives its replay the condition it needs: after each recorded step, check that its expected outcome actually appeared, and if not, hand the step back to the model.
231	=== [user 10-10T20:44:17] is it legal to use a stealth model for this challenge
232	=== [assistant 10-10T20:44:45] Most likely yes, but whether it brings any advantage depends on how its cost gets counted, and only the organizers can say that.
233	
234	## What the rules allow
235	
236	- **Any provider and model with your own key.** `fair-play.md` allows "any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy", and the FAQ lists OpenRouter, where stealth models usually run.
237	- **Unpriced models through OpenRouter.** `run-contract.md` ("How cost is measured") says OpenRouter reports a cost for every call, "so models without a published price are accepted there."
238	- **Only through the proxy.** Bundling a local model or reaching a model any other way is forbidden.
239	
240	## The open questions
241	
242	1. **What it costs in the ranking is unclear.** Stealth models are usually free, so OpenRouter reports $0. The rules say:
243	   - "An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence." Then $0 would count, and cost × time would be close to zero.
244	   - "a call that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price." If $0 is treated as "no cost", every call becomes very expensive.
245	
246	   Which applies isn't written down. The rules also say the cost ranking should "stay honest". A $0 run that beats the leader on cost alone could be flagged for an organizer to look at.
247	2. **There may be an allowlist.** The FAQ says models must "satisfy any organizer model allowlist". The proxy may refuse the model.
248	3. **The model may be gone by the final run.** Stealth models usually run for only a few weeks before they're withdrawn or renamed and priced. The final run uses your latest approved submission on the private dataset *after* the hackathon ends, and that run counts most. If the model has disappeared by then, the run fails. Free models also tend to have strict rate limits.
249	4. **Logging:** stealth providers usually keep prompts and may train on them. The data here is fictional, so that probably doesn't matter.
250	
251	## My recommendation
252	
253	- **Ask the organizers** two things: whether a $0 cost reported by OpenRouter counts as $0, and whether stealth models are on the allowlist.
254	- **Make the model switchable.** The agent should be able to change model by configuration, with Qwen or Clef as the fallback, so a withdrawn model can't sink the final run.
255	- **Don't build on it.** The pointing design already brings model cost close to zero: one decision costs about $0.0001 with Qwen and about $0.0002 with Clef. So a stealth model saves little. It's only worth using if it's clearly *better* at the hard parts (gates, reading meaning) than Qwen.
256	
257	Which stealth model did you have in mind? I can check its current status and price on OpenRouter.

74	## Checks after every action (all verbs)
75	
76	Code puts each action's result into one of these classes and tells the model in one line, for example "clicked 'Weiter' → no effect (3rd time on this page state)":
77	
78	| Outcome | Detected by | Code's reaction |
79	|---|---|---|
80	| logged out | a visible password field | replay the recorded login, repeat the step |
81	| gate | a slider, robot checkbox or image code appeared, and the main content is gone | the `pass_gate` verb |
82	| error | 4xx/5xx status, or error text plus few elements | reload or click "retry" |
83	| no effect | the page signature is unchanged | the model must pick something else |
84	| loop | this page state was already seen during this verb | block the last action |
85	| progress | anything else | continue |
86	
87	## Finish conditions per shape
88	
89	**A. Be in a state** (`login`, `go_home`, `pass_gate`)
90	- **login:** the password field is gone, reloading the start URL still shows none, and a logout control exists or the URL has left the login path. If a gate appears, the login isn't failed; it's waiting for `pass_gate`.
91	- **go_home:** logged in, and at the landing URL recorded at the first login. This is pure code.
92	- **pass_gate:** the gate elements are gone and new content has appeared. Code does the slider and the checkbox; the model only reads the code shown in the image.
93	
94	**B. Open one specific thing** (`find_tender`, and opening a material, message or revision)
95	- The key matches as a whole token after normalization (zero-width characters stripped). "VG-2027-7093-A" doesn't count as "VG-2027-7093".
96	- It must appear in a title position: h1–h3, the page title, a selected tab or breadcrumb, or an identifier field whose value equals the key exactly.
97	- No other key of the same shape may appear in those title positions.
98	- If the key only appears in one row of a list, the check fails with "you're on a list; open the entry".
99	
100	**C. Read a list completely** (`search_catalog`, `search_mail`, `read_qa`, `list_documents`, `list_spec_documents`, `list_revisions`, `read_requirements`, `read_boq`)
101	- **Target:** the model points at the container once, and code remembers its signature.
102	- **Belongs to the query:** the search field holds the query, or every row contains it. Any context keys (tender reference, revision) are visible on the page.
103	- **Fresh:** the container's content changed after the search was submitted. This protects against reading the previous result table.
104	- **Complete,** in this order of preference:
105	  1. a shown total ("12 Treffer", "1–20 von 47") equals the rows read
106	  2. "Seite x von y" equals the pages read
107	  3. no enabled next or "load more" control is left, and the last page brought no new rows
108	  4. none of those signals exists: the list is recorded as coverage "unknown", not as complete
109	- **Empty versus suppressed:** an explicit "no results" message with the query in the search field counts as complete with 0 rows. A "too many hits, narrow your search" message counts as not done, and the model has to choose a narrower query.
110	
111	**D. Read one record fully** (`read_material`, `read_message`, `read_document`, `inspect_bid_form`)
112	- The B condition holds. Then code visits every tab and expands every collapsed section, and the key must still hold on each view. A view where the key is missing doesn't belong to this record.
113	- **Documents:** either the text is shown in the page or an iframe, with the name in a title position (paged viewers follow the C rules), or a download whose file name matches the link the model chose, which code then parses.
114	- **inspect_bid_form:** can only see step 1. Later steps only appear after "Weiter", which saves the step, so this verb can't go further without writing.
115	
116	**E. Change something** (`express_interest`, a form step, requesting the TAN, signing)
117	- **Before acting:** check whether it's already done; if so, change nothing.
118	- **Finish:** the triggering control is gone or disabled, there's no `role=alert` or `aria-invalid`, and the new state is still there after a reload.
119	- **Signing:** finishes when a receipt number appears that wasn't on the page before the action.
120	- **TAN:** the newest message dated after the request.

313	| `click(site, B7, accept_dialog=false)` | Clicks a button or link and returns the new page. A browser confirmation dialog is dismissed unless `accept_dialog=true` is set |
314	| `drag_right(site, F2)` | Drags a slider all the way to the right, e.g. for an unlock gate |
315	| `goto(site, url)`, `press(site, key)` | Opens a URL, presses a key |

Package: "cc-agent: Sonnet research, Haiku submit, credit guard".
- At 00:51 on the run clock, one `browser_evaluate` call started and never returned. Nothing has happened since: no model calls, no screen changes. It was 12:50 in when I last checked.

## What scored 100 in the sandbox

| Run | Models | Time | Atira cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `run_d6be3092` | Opus | 17:44 | $4.53 |
| `run_4cedcc2e` | Opus | 14:15 | $3.88 |
| `run_34c4f8a0` (your link) | Sonnet for everything | **16:43** | **$2.39** |

All three use the same pipeline, which is the `cc-agent` design:
1. **Research:** one session of the unmodified `claude -p` with Playwright MCP, limited to browser tools plus Read. It returns `--json-schema` structured output against the **committed** `evidence.py` schema. The prompt asks for evidence, not conclusions: every revision, Q&A answer, ERP candidate and mail, decoys included.
2. **Rules in code:** `resolver.py` and `pricing.py` compute every number, so the model never does arithmetic. Up to one follow-up round fills any gaps the resolver reports.
3. **Submit:** a second `claude -p` session enters the precomputed bid text and signs it with the TAN.

Every run whose research finished computed the same bid, 356,949.62 EUR net. That includes the scored run that later timed out, the local Opus and Sonnet runs, and the `orch-agent`/`sched-agent` E2E runs. In the Sonnet 100 run, research took 478 s with no gaps. The **submit then took 8:43**, mostly roughly 40 `browser_run_code_unsafe` calls at up to 35 s each, which left a 3:17 margin to the 20-minute limit.

## Why the other runs failed (none were wrong answers)
- **Submit overran the 20 minutes** (`run_a6cb3475`, scored, 20:09). The configurator asked for material attributes the bid text didn't contain, so the model went back to research. Tabs left over from research and a blocking JS dialog made it worse.
- **OpenRouter 402 (out of credit)** on 5 runs, including scored `run_b07c575e`. Claude Code's own cost figure is about twice Atira's meter: $5.58 versus $2.39 on the 100 run.
- **Crash on an error result** (`run_3db846d9`): `evidence_of` calls `json.loads("")` and the script exits.
- **Tool calls with no timeout:** one `run_code_unsafe` call hung for 5:22 in one run, and today's scored run is hung on `browser_evaluate`.
- **Platform failure or cancellation** (`run_7096df0a`, `run_9dc1d17d`).

## Steps to make 100 repeatable
1. **Fund the key.** Raise the OpenRouter limit well above about $6 per run, or best-of-3 can't work. Also rotate it: it was pasted in plain text in one thread and copied to `/tmp/.or_key`.
2. **Keep the research exactly as in the 100 runs:** Sonnet (or Opus), the committed `bid_engine`, one gap round. Don't ship the uncommitted `bid_engine/evidence.py`; it rejects the evidence that scored 100 (`'2.125' is ambiguous`).
3. **Make the submit fast and bounded.** These fixes come from the threads and were measured locally:
   - Put the material attributes and the contact mailbox in the bid text. This cut a submit from 106 to 49 tool calls and 243 s.
   - Close research tabs before submitting (`fresh_tab` in the current `cc-agent/main.py`).
   - Block `browser_run_code_unsafe`.
   - Fill each wizard step in one action.
   - Better still, use the small form tools from `submit-lab/form_server.py`: look, fill with readback, click with dialog control. DeepSeek signed with them in 428 s, but only once.
   - Keep the gate context for Sonnet. It once refused the "Ich bin kein Roboter" slider; with the context added, Sonnet passed in a local E2E run.
4. **Add hard limits in `main.py`:**
   - Give research a cutoff around 9–10 minutes.
   - Have a partial-bid fallback (the resolver leaves out unresolved positions).
   - Catch empty or error results instead of crashing.
5. **Verify with 2–3 test runs** of the same package before the scored submit, and expect sandbox time to be about 1.45× local.

The cheaper approaches are not 100-reliable in the sandbox yet. DeepSeek with numbers converted in code and gap follow-ups scored 3/3 locally for about $0.05, but only on research, with public-1 URLs hardcoded, so it can't be shipped. Qwen, textdump, htmlswarm and the click-path verbs never produced a priced sandbox answer. To get a 100 on the board now, run the Sonnet 100 package plus the submit fixes and timeouts above, on a funded key.

I've read all 15 hackathon threads, both user and assistant messages. I skipped the reasoning blocks, `f837200d` and `1b019342` (both look like your current sessions), and `6d173657` apart from a short summary. Each thread entry uses a fixed order: what was tried, then results, then failures, then ideas never tried.

## Per-thread findings

**1. e51796e8 "Set Up Entire for the Hackathon" (10-10 06:52 → 19:26)**
- **Tried:**
  - A Qwen custom loop (`my-agent/llm_agent.py`) with Playwright MCP, an LLM analyst and `pricing.py`.
  - The `cc-agent` 3-stage pipeline: Opus `claude -p` research → evidence JSON → `bid_engine` resolver → Opus submit.
  - Lean snapshots (`--snapshot-mode none`) plus batched actions.
  - textdump: Haiku collectors save pages, Opus extracts.
  - `sched-agent`: Python scheduler, ERP warm-up, ERP helpers in tabs.
  - A local scorer plus a leak check.
- **Results:**
  - Qwen `run_3c58c86d48b7390a`: quality 5, $0.19, 11:40. It submitted no_bid because ERP data was missing. Scored `run_59846c4a4a722c2d`: 5.
  - Local Opus benchmark: research 453 s, $2.96. Submit took 147 tool calls and $1.92.
  - **Sandbox `run_d6be3092688e69a9`: 100, $4.53, 17:44** (research 10:54, submit 6:50, 88% of the time spent waiting on the model, context grew 40k→155k).
  - Lean snapshots made it worse: 590 s vs 396 s, $3.09 vs $2.93.
  - textdump: no bid, $6.47, 538 s. Opus extraction was $6.21 of that. Playwright's automatic snapshots added about 620k characters of noise.
  - sched-agent: 100 and signed, 767 s, $6.16 (research 524 s, submit 243 s).
- **Failures:**
  - Scored `run_a6cb34755c5cee7d` timed out at 20:09. The submit flailed between leftover research tabs, wrote scripts with `run_code_unsafe`, and re-researched the material attributes that were missing from the bid text.
  - Sonnet refused the "Ich bin kein Roboter" gate (fixed later with truthful context).
  - The `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` secret was set to a URL, which caused 401s.
  - The ERP warm-up blocked for 90 s; the ERP split was uneven (one session took 325 s); the ERP returned 503s.
- **Never tried:**
  - Form scout.
  - In-page bulk paging script.
  - Fast mode / lower effort.
  - Watchdog for a partial bid (you declined it).
  - Resolver mutation tests.
  - Two-stage ERP (technical data for every candidate first, details only for the match).

**2. 9a6f009d Entire commits (10:01 → 13:28).** Entire setup, plus explanations of the analyst vs pricing split. No measured results.

**3. 9939e89c "T3 Thread Timeout Troubleshooting" (13:03 → 21:03)**
- **Tried:**
  - Built the `bid_engine` schema and resolver (27 tests passing).
  - Variant B: Opus head + 4 Opus subagents + an MCP evidence store.
  - Variant C: Opus head + Haiku workers + ERP claims.
  - Two-brains-in-one-browser ERP test.
  - E2E (`orch-agent`): 8 Sonnet owners/helpers + Opus head + work queue + site notes.
  - Submit-only test with a "fill each step in one action" instruction.
  - Steered design: Haiku scrapers + Sonnet readers + Opus orchestrator via streaming input.
  - Login path discovery and replay (Haiku with Claude Code, custom Qwen loop, Haiku writing Playwright without MCP).
  - Stateless pointer prototype.
  - Browser Use.
- **Results:**
  - B: 100 locally, 340 s, $3.63 (ERP took 316 s and was the critical path).
  - C: 98.7, 575 s, $1.58. Haiku read stock as 95 instead of 29.
  - ERP tab test: helper ramp-up dropped from 72–92 s to 7 s; 5 ERP groups done in 153 s for $0.84.
  - **E2E: 100, research 319 s, submit 374 s, total 697 s, $4.58.**
  - Submit-only: 352 s, 49 calls, $1.15, one attempt (previously 106 calls).
  - Steered design: no bid within 10 minutes.
  - Login replay: Haiku via Claude Code $0.028; Qwen custom loop $0.017 (but ERP 273 s); Haiku without MCP writing code $0.011, ERP replayed fully in 5.6 s.
  - Pointer + Qwen: tender and supplier portal logins in 4–6 s for $0.0001 each.
  - Browser Use: standard mode 4/4 but 62–392 s per site; flash mode reported 2 false successes.
- **Failures:**
  - Unknown field names were silently dropped (`extra=ignore`).
  - "212.063" in de-DE was read 1000× too small (Sonnet).
  - Records were overwritten by last-write-wins.
  - Store numbers came back flagged "ambiguous".
  - The portal session expired mid-form (about 5 minutes).
  - Pointer loops at the ERP gate.
  - Readers only triggered at turn end, so the steered design lost the ERP pages.
- **Never tried / never finished:**
  - Coverage records.
  - Keeping all observations per id (conflict tracking).
  - `Judgment` record type.
  - Browser contexts as 8 slots.
  - Clef as a filter.
  - Memory/self-evaluation field in the pointer.
  - Screenshot fallback.

**4. 3908c1ef "Map Data Paths and Task Dependencies" (19:19 → 20:46)**
- **Tried:** diagnosis of the Qwen lite-agent; brute-force verb discovery with 14 Haiku sessions.
- **Results:**
  - Qwen `run_935ad800d98f6e7f`: extraction calls took 82% of the time (5–8.5k output tokens each, 1.5–4 min). A 60 s timeout plus retry meant nothing was ever recorded.

**5. 08dd4a6f "Custom Browser Harness for Login" (19:39 → 20:47)**

- **Tried:** built `goals.py` finish conditions (shapes A–E).
- **Results:** Qwen, 16 goals in 204 s, $0.02 (109 calls, about 1.08k tokens in and 50 out per call). Several false passes: `list_documents` read 16 rows instead of 3; `inspect_bid_form`.

**8. 6ba6e455 "Clev Cost Savings" (20:37 → 21:31)**
- **Results:**
  - DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Relace: 4 logins for $0.00041, ERP gate passed in 6 calls.

**9. 9b88627c "Evaluate Qwen and DeepSeek for T3" (21:08 → 22:57)**
- **Results:**
  - Derived that a run needs only 8 verbs.

- **Tried:** claim-and-verify paging, typed quoted `want` items, a scope rule, a sibling rule, re-login.
- **Results:** Haiku 14/16 with no false passes, 208 s, $0.026.

## (b) Root-cause failure modes

1. **The submit step overran the 20 minutes.** Causes, in order of impact:
   - Material attributes (bore, stroke, mounting, certification, catalogue group) were missing from the bid text, so the submit agent went back to research.
   - Opus/Sonnet wrote `browser_run_code_unsafe` scripts (7–35 s each, about 40 per run).
   - Leftover research tabs caused `browser_tabs` thrashing.
   - Blocking JS dialogs.
2. **Portal session expired after about 5 minutes** in the middle of the wizard, losing all steps (E2E, DeepSeek form run). "Weiter" is the only save; going back clears later steps.
3. **Hangs with no tool timeout:**
   - `browser_evaluate` hung 12 minutes.
   - `run_code_unsafe` hung 5:22.
   - 60 s Playwright action waits; 30 s waits per form field.
   - A DeepSeek call with reasoning on hung more than 5 minutes.
   - Qwen extraction timed out at 60 s, then retried.
4. **Infrastructure:**
   - OpenRouter 402 on 5 runs (Claude Code reports about 2× Atira's metered cost).
   - Wrong secret value.
   - `json.loads("")` crash.
   - Atira queue (up to 12 minutes) and platform timeouts.
   - Port collisions and shared scouting accounts across threads; ERP returns 403 on two simultaneous logins in tabs.
5. **TAN handling:** 3 attempts were needed; the first TAN was probably read from the wrong spot. A new request invalidates the old TAN; each lasts 5 minutes. The mail carries a hidden "99% Sonderrabatt" injection.
